analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and tax on large inherited wealth transfers.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the estate tax never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Ways and Means Committee when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated the federal tax on estates left when someone dies, the tax on large gifts, and the tax on transfers that skip a generation (for example, a grandparent leaving money directly to a grandchild). Only estates large enough to owe the tax — at the time, estates worth more than $600,000 — would benefit. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to very large estates. In 1997, the estate tax applied only to estates above a $600,000 exemption, so the bill's entire benefit would go to families passing on large amounts of wealth. Wealth-advisory businesses would also gain new planning opportunities in the absence of the tax, though repeal would eliminate much of the estate-planning work the tax creates.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the entire estate tax chapter of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the tax on estates of people dying after enactment. [S3] [S2]
It also repeals the gift tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, applying to transfers made after enactment, so large gifts and bequests to grandchildren would be tax-free as well. [S3]
Under the law in effect in 1997, only estates larger than the $600,000 exemption owed any estate tax, so the repeal's benefits would go entirely to the largest inheritances. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes raise revenue that funds the government; repealing them would either require other taxes to rise, spending to fall, or deficits to grow, with the lost revenue replaced by taxes on people who do not own multimillion-dollar estates.

drawbacks.text: Repeal removes a tax that falls exclusively on the largest estates and is one of the most progressive parts of the tax code; the lost revenue would have to be replaced by taxes on a much broader base of taxpayers. [S2] [S3]
Because the bill contains no offsetting revenue, enacting it would have increased federal deficits or forced cuts or tax increases elsewhere. [S3]
The bill would also eliminate the gift tax, which prevents taxpayers from avoiding income and transfer taxes by giving wealth away while alive; repealing it opens a new avoidance channel. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated: tax-free inheritance for heirs of estates over roughly $600,000 — a small fraction of families in 1997. The cost is spread across everyone else through higher other taxes, lower spending, or larger deficits to make up the lost revenue. The bill contained no revenue offsets and no provisions aimed at families of ordinary means, so its costs to the general public outweighed its benefits for most people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Philip Crane, joined by Representative Hulshof, introduced the bill on February 4, 1997 to repeal the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax. [S3] [S1]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the committee took no further action on it during the 105th Congress. [S5] [S1]
Ten Republican representatives cosponsored the bill, but it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote. [S4] [S5]
The bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, leaving the estate and gift taxes on the books. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate and gift taxes remained in place, so the federal Treasury kept the revenue and heirs to multimillion-dollar estates did not get the tax-free inheritance the bill would have provided. General taxpayers were spared replacing that revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; the estate tax survived

for.name: Rep. Philip M. Crane
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.

for.name: Rep. Kenny Hulshof
for.what_they_did: Joined Crane in introducing the bill.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting the bill die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 10 cosponsors were Republicans; the bill got no Democratic support and no floor action of any kind.

industries.note: Repeal would have eliminated taxes on inheritances and large gifts, a benefit flowing only to estates above the roughly $600,000 exemption in effect in 1997. The lost revenue would fall on other taxpayers. [S2] [S3]
Repeal of the estate and gift taxes would eliminate much of the planning work the taxes create, but it would also open new opportunities around the surviving income-tax rules. [S3]
